paras: The attempted lynching at Danville, Arkansas, was a failed attempt by a mob in early September 1881 to break into the Yell County jail at Danville and hang three prisoners accused of murder, named in the reports as Bruce, Taylor and Burris. Warned in advance, the sheriff chained the prisoners together and hid them in the woods overnight while the mob searched for them in vain. The episode was reported chiefly as a prelude to what followed two days later, when a mob took Taylor and Bruce from the jail at Dardanelle and hanged them.

The three men were held on murder charges, and the Chicago Tribune's Little Rock correspondent wrote that the lives of Taylor and Bruce had been repeatedly threatened since their jailing and that they had been moved from place to place to avoid lynching. A Little Rock special to the Memphis Daily Appeal said Bruce was accused of cutting the throat of a young man named White near Dardanelle the previous winter after a dispute at a camp, and that Burris was accused of murdering a man named Sturtevant. None of the reports gives the race of the three prisoners.

According to the Tribune, on the Thursday night before the Dardanelle hanging, about September 8, the sheriff of Yell County received a hint that a mob meant to break into the Danville jail and hang the three men. He took the prisoners out, chained them together and kept them at a secluded spot in the woods until daylight. The mob went to the jail, found it empty, and spent the rest of the night beating the forest in the hope of finding the sheriff and his prisoners, without success. The Batesville Guard, an Arkansas weekly, described the night as an attempt "by a large mob" to execute the prisoners that was foiled by the sheriff removing them "beyond the reach of the mob."

After that night the prisoners were separated, with Taylor and Bruce put in the jail at Dardanelle and Burris in the jail at Dover. The Russellville Democrat explained that Burris had been sent to Dover on a change of venue to Pope County. On the following Saturday night, a mob that the Tribune put at nearly a hundred men rode into Dardanelle, took Taylor and Bruce from the jail and hanged them from a tree in nearby timber.

Burris escaped that night because he was not in the Dardanelle jail. The Memphis Appeal passed on a report that he was to be lynched at Dover, while the Tribune's correspondent wrote that he was "yet alive" but expected to share his companions' fate. No report of arrests or of any inquiry into the Danville attempt appears in the coverage.

Only white papers covered the episode, and most of them mentioned the Danville night only as background to the Dardanelle lynching. The Tribune's special ran under a headline about murderers "Taken from an Arjnmsas Jail and Hanged by a Mob," called the prisoners "murderers," and ended by stating that "Public opinion Is with the lynchers" because of the weak administration of law in the courts. The Batesville Guard, by contrast, gave the attempt a single sentence that credited the "prompt action of the sheriff" and said nothing of the later hanging.

Ten days after the Guard, the Donaldsonville Chief in Louisiana carried a one-line item among its domestic briefs about the sheriff chaining "three murderers" in the woods to protect them. None of these reports used racial terms for the prisoners or for the mob.

The reports disagree on the jail: the Tribune and the Batesville Guard place it at Danville, while the Donaldsonville Chief names Dardanelle. Danville is the better-supported location, since the two detailed and nearer reports agree on it and Dardanelle was where Taylor and Bruce were held and hanged afterward.

chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A mob went to the Danville jail intending to hang three prisoners held for murder and searched the woods for them all night, an attempted lynching that failed (A1, A3).
No one was killed in the Danville episode: the sheriff hid the prisoners and the mob did not find them (A1, A3); the hanging of Taylor and Bruce two days later at Dardanelle is a separate episode.

The Chicago Tribune's Little Rock special (A1) and the Arkansas Batesville Guard (A3) independently report the mob's foiled attempt at the Danville jail; the Donaldsonville Chief (A13) agrees on the sheriff hiding the men in the woods but names Dardanelle.

framing.detail: The Tribune called the prisoners 'murderers', told the Danville night as a lead-in to the 'ghastly' Dardanelle hanging, and closed that public opinion was with the lynchers because of weak courts.
The Batesville Guard reported the attempt in one sentence, crediting the 'prompt action of the sheriff'.
The Donaldsonville Chief ran a one-line item among domestic briefs calling the men 'three murderers'.
